title: Area III review: Preflight Preparation
intro: These questions mix the three Tasks of Area III: weather information, cross-country flight planning and the instrument flight deck check. Most join them in one IFR lesson, such as a forecast that drives the alternate and the fuel, an icing plan that starts with the freezing level graphic, a void time that tempts a learner to rush the gyros, or a cold-temperature approach that turns on which thermometer to believe.

questions.q: Twenty miles from her destination, your instrument learner compares two reports. The METAR she got through FIS-B 15 minutes ago gave wind 250 at 12 and 5 SM; the ASOS broadcast she now hears gives wind 240 at 12 and visibility 3. She is choosing her approach and asks whether the ASOS is broken. What do you teach?
options: Trust the METAR: one-minute broadcast data are raw and show improving weather faster than worsening weather
Both winds are magnetic, so the 10° change is a real wind shift, and a SPECI should follow within minutes
Nothing is broken: the broadcast is one-minute data with wind in magnetic degrees, while FIS-B uses true
The broadcast wind is true and the METAR wind magnetic, so she adds the variation before picking a runway
questions.why: ASOS broadcasts can differ from the METAR seen on the internet or FIS-B, because the broadcast is the one-minute observation data, and its averaging reports deteriorating conditions much quicker than improving ones [[28:287|AWH 24-3]]. So the lower visibility is likely the newer picture, not a fault, and the METAR-first option has the averaging backward. National distribution such as FSS, the internet and FIS-B gives wind in true degrees, while local radio and telephone give it in magnetic degrees [[28:287|AWH 24-3]], so 250 true and 240 magnetic can be the same wind; the option with the two references swapped is the tempting trap. A wind shift SPECI needs a change of 45° or more in less than 15 minutes with 10 knots or more [[28:290|AWH 24-6]], so 10° is not one. Application: for runway and approach choice, have her use the broadcast's magnetic wind and its visibility.

questions.q: An hour before an IFR departure, your learner finds her route passing 30 NM southeast of a Convective SIGMET polygon issued at 1755Z. The text reads AREA TS MOV FROM 31030KT TOPS ABV FL400, and she will be abeam the area at about 1900Z. She calls it a non-factor because the polygon does not touch her route. What do you teach?
options: The polygon is a snapshot at 55 past the hour; moving from 310° at 30 kt, the storms may reach her route by then
She is right: a Convective SIGMET covers only its polygon, which is drawn to allow for movement over its valid time
It matters only if the text says severe; a plain area of thunderstorms implies moderate turbulence and no icing
She may go and use datalink radar to thread the cells if they drift close, since the image shows them in real time
questions.why: The Convective SIGMET polygon is a snapshot of the area at its issuance time of 55 minutes past the hour. During the valid time the area moves with the vector in the text, fast-moving areas will very likely end up outside the polygon by the end of the hour, and the graphic should be compared with the text and used only for strategic planning [[28:374|AWH 26-7]]. Moving from 310° at 30 knots, an hour of movement uses up her 30 NM margin. Any Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear, whether or not the text says severe [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]. Datalinked radar shows where precipitation was and may be 15 to 20 minutes older than its time stamp [[28:327|AWH 24-43]], and FIS weather supports strategic decisions, not negotiating a path through a hazard area [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]. Application: have her re-plan the route around the area before she files.

questions.q: Planning tomorrow's IFR trip in the club's single, which is not approved for icing, your learner sees a hatched area on the freezing level forecast graphic over her destination, where light rain is forecast with a surface temperature of -1 °C. Her plan if ice forms on the descent is to go lower, because it is always warmer down low. What do you teach?
options: Hatching shows the whole column below freezing, so no liquid water can exist there and icing on the descent is unlikely
Hatching marks missing model data, so she should take the freezing level from the FB forecast instead and keep her plan
Her plan is sound, since the hatching shows only where the surface is above freezing, which confirms warmer air below
Hatching means a below-freezing surface with more than one freezing level aloft, so the warm layer may be above her
questions.why: On the freezing level graphics, hatched or spotted regions are areas where the surface is below freezing with multiple freezing levels aloft; white, not hatching, means the surface and the whole depth of the atmosphere are below freezing [[28:454|AWH 27-53]] [[28:365|AWH 25-23]]. When ice forms, the two ways out are to leave the precipitation or go to an altitude where the temperature is above freezing, and that warmer altitude may not always be a lower one [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]. AC 91-74B calls the freezing levels, inversions and multiple freezing levels critical to deciding how to exit icing [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1c]], and asks pilots to settle during preflight whether a climb or a descent will be a workable exit [[38:45|AC 91-74B 5-4a(3)]]. The FB forecast does give an approximate freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]], but that does not make the hatching missing data.

questions.q: Forty miles out on an IFR flight, your learner's FIS-B display shows the destination METAR from 40 minutes ago: OVC014 6SM. Approach control then reads her the current ATIS: OVC006 2SM BR. She had planned her approach on the METAR and says the datalink must be right because it is the official report. What do you teach?
options: Plan on the FIS-B METAR, since datalinked products are the official record and ATC voice weather is only advisory
Plan on the controller's report: when FIS and voice differ, use the most recent data from the most authoritative source
Plan on the METAR until a SPECI shows on her display, since a falling ceiling is never a SPECI trigger once below 1,500 ft
Plan on the FIS-B METAR, since an ATIS is redone only once an hour and so is older than any report on her display
questions.why: When FIS information and information from ATC or FSS by voice differ, the AIM cautions pilots to use the most recent data from the most authoritative source, and says FIS should not be the sole source of weather in flight [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]. An ATIS must be updated on receipt of any official hourly and special weather report [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]], so it is not limited to once an hour. A ceiling falling through 1,000 ft is itself a SPECI criterion [[28:290|AWH 24-6]], so the drop from 1,400 to 600 would bring a special report that her 40-minute-old datalink copy cannot show. Application: her approach briefing, fuel check and any diversion decision now start from the 600 and 2 she just heard.

questions.q: Your learner now flies a single approved for flight in known icing. Her route crosses a SIGMET for severe icing from 5,000 to 9,000 ft, with AIRMET Zulu around it. She says the SIGMET does not apply to her, because the airplane is certified for known ice and its system checked fine on the run-up. What do you teach?
options: She is right: icing SIGMETs are written for airplanes without ice protection, and AIRMET Zulu covers the equipped ones only
A severe icing SIGMET applies to all aircraft, and severe icing lies outside the certification envelope: route around it
She may go if a jet in the area reports only light ice, because a recent PIREP overrides an icing SIGMET for her type
She may go if the system checks good again before takeoff, since certification covers every intensity in a SIGMET
questions.why: Severe icing is one of the SIGMET criteria [[28:372|AWH 26-5]], and AC 91-74B says a SIGMET for severe icing applies to all aircraft, from small GA aircraft to transport jets [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1d]]. The IFH warns pilots of airplanes certificated for flight in known icing that severe icing is a condition outside the certification icing envelope [[23:92|IFH 4-15]], and the AIM describes severe icing as a rate at which ice protection systems fail to remove the ice [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]. A run-up check shows the system works, not that it can handle severe ice. A jet's report is a poor guide for her airplane, because the ram air temperature rise can mask icing for high-speed aircraft, while small low-speed airplanes give the most accurate reports [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1e]].

questions.q: Your learner plans an IFR flight on a true course of 270° at 9,000 ft, in IFR conditions with an alternate required. The FB forecast at 9,000 ft reads 2730-04. Her POH gives a true airspeed of 130 knots at 10 gallons per hour. The destination is 150 NM away and the alternate 25 NM beyond it on the same course. Not counting start, taxi and climb fuel, what does 91.167 require?
options: About 21 gallons: the 130-knot true airspeed sets the time, because FB winds are already applied in true degrees
About 18 gallons: 2730 is a wind blowing toward 270°, a 30-knot tailwind that gives a 160-knot groundspeed
About 22.5 gallons: the two legs at a 100-knot groundspeed, plus a 30-minute reserve at normal cruise under IFR
About 25 gallons: 1.75 hours to the alternate at a 100-knot groundspeed, plus 45 minutes at normal cruising speed
questions.why: In the FB code DDff+TT the direction is true, in tens of degrees, and the speed is in knots [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]; the PHAK decodes such a group as the wind from that direction [[1:323|PHAK 13-13]]. So 2730-04 is a wind from 270° at 30 knots with -4 °C, a direct headwind on a 270° true course. Groundspeed is true airspeed adjusted for wind and decreases with a headwind [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]], so it is 100 knots, and groundspeed, not true airspeed, sets the time and fuel when there is wind [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. 91.167 requires fuel to the destination, then to the alternate, then for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(3)]]: 175 NM at 100 knots is 1.75 hours, plus 0.75 is 2.5 hours, or 25 gallons. Thirty minutes is not the IFR reserve. The -04 also warns her that any cloud at 9,000 ft would be icing cloud [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]].

questions.q: Your learner's airplane has an approach-approved WAAS GPS. Her destination needs an alternate, and she picks one whose only approach is an RNAV (GPS) with LPV and LNAV lines and standard alternate minimums. Its TAF for her ETA there reads FM151800 18008KT 4SM -RA OVC007. Does it qualify?
options: Yes: the LPV gives vertical guidance like an ILS, so the 600 ft and 2 SM precision standard applies, and 700 ft meets it
No: with WAAS she plans the LNAV or circling line with nonprecision weather, 800 and 2, so 700 ft falls short
No: a GPS approach may be planned at the destination or at the alternate but never at both, whatever the receiver
Yes: WAAS users may plan the LPV line at any alternate where the A NA symbol has been removed from the chart
questions.why: TAF cloud heights are in hundreds of feet AGL, and the lowest BKN, OVC or VV layer is the ceiling, so OVC007 is a 700 ft ceiling [[28:415|AWH 27-14]]. When using WAAS at an alternate, flight planning must be based on the LNAV or circling minima line with the part 91 nonprecision weather requirements; LPV may be used on arrival if the receiver shows it is available [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18]]. With no published alternate minimums, nonprecision means 800 ft and 2 SM [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)(i)(B)]], and approaches with vertical guidance are nonprecision approaches for this rule [[29:146|IPH 4-6]], which is why the ILS comparison fails. Removing the A NA symbol lets WAAS receivers use the procedure at an alternate; it does not allow planning on the LPV line [[33:105|AIM 1-1-18]]. The destination-or-alternate limit applies to TSO-C129 and C196 users, not to WAAS users [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]].

questions.q: Your learner is IFR at 6,000 ft in stratus in the club's single, which is not approved for icing; the MEA is 5,000 ft. A Cessna 182 PIREP from earlier read /SK OVC025-TOP070 /TA M06 /IC LGT RIME, and the freezing level was forecast at 2,000 ft. Now the OAT reads -4 °C, rime is building on the strut, and the frequency is busy. What do you coach?
options: Declare an emergency, tell ATC she is climbing above the reported 7,000-ft tops, and exit without awaiting a clearance
Ask for lower and hold 6,000 until cleared, because an IFR pilot may never leave an assigned altitude without a clearance
Descend at once to 2,000 ft to get under the freezing level, since descending is always the fastest route to warmer air
Engage the autopilot in vertical speed mode for a gentle climb, so she can watch the ice while it flies the airplane
questions.why: An airplane not certificated for icing that meets ice should exit as expeditiously as possible and declare an emergency, telling ATC what the pilot is doing; when a clearance may not come in time, AC 91-74B recommends declaring an emergency and exiting as soon as practical [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. The PIREP puts the tops at 7,000 ft MSL [[28:313|AWH 24-29]], and because icing in stratiform cloud is often a thin layer, a climb may take the airplane out of the cloud altogether [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1h]]. A descent to 2,000 ft would take her below the 5,000-ft MEA [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(1)]], and the warmer altitude may not always be a lower one [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. Vertical speed is the least desirable autopilot mode in icing and should not be used [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]]. Afterward she reports the icing to ATC with her aircraft type [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].

questions.q: At 0600 the METAR reads 00000KT 10SM SKC M04/M06 A3021. The club single sat outside all night and has a thin, even frost on the wings. Your learner plans to brush off what she can reach and let the rest blow off on the takeoff roll. The FBO offers its heated hangar for 40 minutes. What do you hold her to?
options: A thin, even frost is acceptable on a light single if she holds the airplane on the runway a few knots past rotation speed
This cannot be frost, since frost forms only under a cloud deck; on a clear night it must be harmless dew and can stay
All of it comes off before flight; if she uses the hangar, the airplane must be dry before it goes back out into the cold
Use the hangar, then taxi out right away while the wings are still wet, since melted frost cannot refreeze on a warm skin
questions.why: The METAR shows a calm, clear morning at -4 °C with a dewpoint of -6 °C [[28:302|AWH 24-18]], and frost forms on an airplane sitting outside on a clear night when moisture is present and the skin cools below freezing by radiation [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4b]]. Even very small amounts of frost, snow or ice may hurt the wing, so all of it is removed before flight; a heated hangar works, but the airplane must be dry before it comes out so the water does not refreeze [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]]. The figure shows why: upper surface frost lowers the most lift the wing can make, and the IFH says any accumulation of ice or frost should be removed before attempting flight [[23:92|IFH 4-15]]. No source gives a speed margin that makes frost acceptable.

questions.q: Your learner filed G in Item 10a with NAV/SBAS, a route on T-routes and the RNAV (GPS) LPV at her destination, which also has an ILS. At the run-up the GPS navigator shows a failure and no position. Her VOR/ILS receiver passed a VOT check last week, and the ceiling is 700 overcast. What does she do?
options: Depart as filed and mention it only if ATC clears her onto a T-route, since the filed codes are kept for search and rescue
Depart as filed and fly the T-routes on the VOR, since T-routes and Victor airways share the same MEAs and route structure
Cancel the flight, because a PBN aircraft cannot fly IFR without its GPS even with a VOR receiver that passed its check
Advise ATC and amend her equipment, then take a route she can fly on VOR to the ILS, since ATC expects what she filed
questions.why: If GPS avionics become inoperative, the pilot should advise ATC and amend the equipment suffix [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. ATC issues clearances based on the capabilities filed in Items 10 and 18 and expects the pilot to use a capability that is filed [[33:332|AIM 5-1-6]]. T-routes require GPS or GPS/WAAS equipment [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]], so the VOR cannot fly them. The part kept for search and rescue and not sent to ATC is Item 19 [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4]], not Item 10. Nothing stops the airplane from flying IFR on the VOR and ILS: a VOR used under IFR needs a check within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]], which she has, and the navigation equipment need only be suitable for the route [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(2)]].

questions.q: The approach charts for your learner's destination show a snowflake with -15 °C. Ten minutes out, the destination ASOS reports -17 °C, while her OAT gauge at the 4,000-ft initial approach altitude reads -23 °C. Which temperature decides the cold temperature correction, and what follows?
options: Her OAT reading of -23 °C, because the error comes from the air the airplane flies through, so she corrects all segments
The airport's reported -17 °C, which is at or below -15 °C, so she corrects and coordinates any intermediate change with ATC
Neither: the snowflake applies only to baro-VNAV approaches, so she flies the charted altitudes on any other approach
The airport's reported -17 °C, but she corrects only the final segment, and ATC must approve each of the corrected altitudes there
questions.why: Cold temperature corrections are based on the temperature at the reporting station, not the temperature observed at the airplane's altitude [[23:101|IFH 5-6]], so the OAT gauge is the tempting wrong source. The snowflake and temperature are a Cold Temperature Airport limitation published on every IAP for the airfield, separate from the baro-VNAV temperature limit; at or below that temperature, pilots should calculate corrections for the appropriate segments [[33:341|AIM 5-1-17]]. Planned corrections for the intermediate or missed approach holding segments must be coordinated with ATC, while a final segment correction needs no advice to ATC [[33:342|AIM 5-1-17]]. In planning, the AIM has pilots request the lowest forecast temperature for 1 hour either side of arrival [[33:341|AIM 5-1-17]], so this decision can begin at the briefing.

questions.q: Your learner's airplane has a WAAS GPS and one VOR/ILS receiver. Her destination needs an alternate, and she picks one whose only approach is a VOR approach with standard alternate minimums; its TAF for her ETA there shows BKN010 4SM. The last VOR check in the logbook is 34 days old, and her departure airport has a VOT. Can this plan work?
options: Yes, once a VOT check finds the receiver within ±4° and she logs the date, place, error and signature; 1,000 and 4 meet 800-2
No: an overdue check grounds the VOR until a repair station recalibrates it, so she needs an alternate with an RNAV approach
Yes, with no check: her WAAS GPS can fly the whole VOR approach in place of the receiver, so 91.171 does not apply to it
Yes, after a VOT check within ±6°, as long as the alternate also forecasts 2,000 and 3 from 1 hour before to 1 hour after
questions.why: A VOR used under IFR must have been checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]]; with a test signal at the airport of intended departure the limit is ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]], and the person checking enters the date, place, bearing error and a signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. Nothing requires a repair station for an overdue check. The GPS may be used on the final segment of a VOR approach only with the VOR operating and monitored, and may not substitute for the VOR giving lateral guidance on final [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]], so the receiver still needs its check. The ±6° limit belongs to an airborne checkpoint [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]. At the alternate only the forecast at the ETA counts: with no published alternate minimums, a nonprecision approach needs 800 ft and 2 SM [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)(i)(B)]], while the 2,000-and-3 test belongs to the destination [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]].

questions.q: Your learner is departing a nontowered Class G airport under a 500-ft overcast. By phone she gets her IFR clearance with a void time 8 minutes away, then starts the engine. The vacuum attitude and heading indicators are still spinning up, and she plans to skip the run-up instrument checks to make the void time. What do you teach?
options: Take off before the void time and finish the gyro checks in the climb, because a void time can never be changed once issued
Take off on time: the clearance is void only if she is still on the ground 30 minutes after the void time has passed
Let the void time pass, tell ATC as soon as possible, and get a new release once the gyros are up and the checks are done
Let the void time pass without calling, since an expired void time cancels the flight plan and she simply files it again
questions.why: A pilot who does not depart before the clearance void time must advise ATC of their intentions as soon as possible, within the time ATC allows, which cannot exceed 30 minutes, or the aircraft is considered overdue and search and rescue starts. An expired void time does not cancel the clearance or the flight plan; it withdraws her authority to depart IFR until a new release is issued [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]. The airplane must be airborne before the void time, not within 30 minutes after it [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. The heading indicator needs about 5 minutes after start to spin up before it is set [[23:132|IFH 5-37]], the attitude indicator normally erects in 2 to 3 minutes and can take 5 [[23:114|IFH 5-19]], and a hasty taxi and run-up that does not let mechanical gyros spool up makes a departure into IMC unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Application: teach her to tell ATC when she expects to be airborne, as the IFH suggests [[23:56|IFH 2-5]], with room for the full check.

questions.q: En route in IMC under IFR, your learner's portable ADS-B In receiver shows a target 300 ft below and closing, and its FIS-B radar shows a gap between two cells 8 NM ahead. She wants to climb 500 ft away from the target and then aim for the gap. What do you teach?
options: Climb but skip the gap: ADS-B traffic is fine for avoidance in IMC, while the radar image may be 15 to 20 minutes old
Aim for the gap but hold altitude: FIS-B radar suits tactical use inside 3 minutes, but the traffic display does not
Do both, then tell ATC: with ADS-B In she has the same traffic picture as the controller, so she may maneuver on her own
Neither: no avoidance maneuvers in IMC on ADS-B traffic, and datalink radar shows where rain was, not a way through
questions.why: The ADS-B cockpit display of traffic is not a collision avoidance system; it must not be used for avoidance maneuvers during IMC or other times without visual contact, and no avoidance maneuvers are authorized because a target is displayed [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]]. FIS weather such as ground-based radar is not appropriate for tactical avoidance, typically under 3 minutes, such as negotiating a path through a hazard area; it supports strategic decisions 20 minutes or more ahead [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]. Datalinked mosaics show where precipitation was and may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the age shown [[28:327|AWH 24-43]], so the gap may already be closed. Application: she asks ATC about the traffic and for a route around the whole area, and keeps to her clearance until she gets one.

questions.q: Your learner now flies a single approved for flight in known icing, and its AFM says nothing about autopilot use in ice. In cruise in light rime, she plans to stay on the autopilot in altitude hold for the whole encounter so she can watch the ice protection. The autopilot passed its preflight test. What do you teach?
options: With the AFM silent, hand-fly it: the autopilot masks the trim and handling changes that tell her ice is building up
Altitude hold is the right mode in ice because it keeps the airspeed constant as drag rises, so she can leave it on
Switch to vertical speed mode, because holding a set climb or descent rate protects the airspeed as the ice builds
Leave it on: it will disconnect early in ice, well before the handling changes, which makes it a useful ice warning
questions.why: Unless the AFM/POH recommends otherwise, the AFH says the autopilot should not be used in icing: continuous use masks the trim and handling changes that come with ice, and the autopilot disconnects suddenly when it reaches its design limits, leaving the pilot with an airplane that may already handle badly [[24:259|AFH 13-10]]. AC 91-74B adds that as ice builds, the autopilot will try to hold altitude without regard for airspeed, leading toward a stall, and that vertical speed is the least desirable mode and should not be used; if workload keeps the autopilot on, monitor it closely for abnormal trim, trim rate or attitude [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]].

questions.q: Your learner plans a GPS-direct IFR leg at night over a designated mountainous area, off airways and outside radar coverage. Her glass-panel single has an MFD terrain page, though no TAWS is required for it. She plans to fly 1,000 ft above the highest terrain the page shows near her course, trusting it to alert her. What do you teach?
options: Her plan works: terrain alerts are based on time to impact, so 1,000 ft over the displayed terrain is all the rule asks
Use the MEA of the nearest airway, because en route chart MEAs apply to any direct route through the same area
The page is an aid, not a primary source; off airways she owns obstacle clearance, 2,000 ft over the highest within 4 NM
Fly the OROCA, since it assures signal and radar coverage as well as 2,000 ft above terrain in mountainous areas
questions.why: AFMs prohibit using the terrain awareness, moving map, traffic and datalink weather displays as the primary data source, though the PHAK suggests the MFD terrain page for night or IMC flight near mountains [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. The AIM reminds pilots that they are responsible for obstruction clearance on direct route segments outside controlled airspace and ATC surveillance, because the MEAs on en route charts pertain to the routes and may not meet obstruction clearance criteria off them [[33:335|AIM 5-1-6]]. Where no minimum altitude is prescribed, 91.177 requires 2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 4 NM of the course over a designated mountainous area [[60:480|14 CFR 91.177(a)(2)(i)]]. A TAWS bases its alerts on time to potential impact [[23:130|IFH 5-35]], which sets no altitude, and TAWS is required only in turbine-powered airplanes with six or more passenger seats [[60:498|14 CFR 91.223(a)]]. The OROCA helps with planning, but it is not assessed for signal, ATC surveillance or communications coverage [[2:71|Chart Users' Guide p 71]].
